Title: Co-occurrence of APC and EGFR L858R mutations in colorectal cancer: A case report
PMID: 
Authors: Vitor Jodar Cavalheiro, Daniel Santos Rocha Sobral Filho, Giulia Mazaro de Oliveira, Manuela del Rio Navarrete da Fonseca, Gabriel Travessini, Ibere Cauduro Soares, Gilberto de Castro Junior, Jorge Sabbaga, Milena Perez Mak, Paulo Marcelo Gehm Hoff

Abstract
Mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene are frequent in colorectal cancer (CRC), whereas epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, particularly the L858R variant, are exceedingly rare. Their coexistence in CRC is rare and poorly described in the literature and poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We describe a 69-year-old man with a history of resected CRC who presented with a lung mass and adrenal lesions, initially suspected as metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Biopsy revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma with immunohistochemistry suggestive of gastrointestinal origin. Due to doubts regarding the primary site, it was decided to start systemic treatment with mFOLFIRINOX while awaiting NGS. After 7 cycles, a partial radiologic and clinical response was observed. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) became available and identified an EGFR L858R mutation, favoring NSCLC. Chemotherapy was paused, and the patient was treated with gefitinib. Rapid disease progression ensued, with new brain metastases. Expanded NGS subsequently revealed concurrent APC and TP53 pathogenic variants, confirming the diagnosis of metastatic CRC harboring co-occurring EGFR and APC mutations. The patient died 10 months after diagnosis. This case underscores the critical role of comprehensive molecular profiling via NGS in accurately diagnosing complex oncologic presentations. To our knowledge, this is the first case report of APC and EGFR L858R co-mutation in colorectal cancer. For this patient, the misclassification delayed the use of more appropriate therapies for CRC, which may have impacted clinical outcomes.

Case presentation
The patient was a 69-year-old male, a former smoker (8 pack-years) until 1993, with a history of localized colorectal adenocarcinoma treated with surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy in 2015. There is no available information regarding the adjuvant treatment administered, as the patient was unable to report the treatment details and the medical records were not accessible. He was discharged from oncology follow-up in 2020 due to the absence of recurrence.
In 2023, the patient presented with a dry cough, right hemithorax pain, and weight loss. He was referred to our oncology center with suspected metastatic lung cancer.
A CT scan (Figure 1A) revealed a neoplastic lesion in the left lower lung lobe, measuring 13.0 × 9.6 × 10.6 cm, with mediastinal lymph node enlargement. The adrenal glands were also enlarged (right: 9.1 cm; left: 7.7 cm) (Figure 1C), with suspicious hepatic nodules. A head CT showed no suspicious lesions. Colonoscopy findings were unremarkable.
Bronchoscopy revealed an obstructive vegetative lesion in the posterior segmental bronchus of the left lower lobe. Biopsy showed poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for AE1/AE3, CK20, and CDX-2 and negative for CK7, chromogranin A, TTF-1, and p63, suggesting either a primary NSCLC with intestinal differentiation or a gastrointestinal primary site.
Due to the inconclusive pathology findings, a multidisciplinary discussion was conducted. Imaging findings favored advanced NSCLC with adrenal involvement, while immunohistochemistry suggested a gastrointestinal origin. Considering the patient’s history, first-line systemic treatment with mFOLFIRINOX (infusional 5-FU, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin) was initiated, as it is active in both lung and colorectal cancer, while awaiting NGS results. Although a standard option would have been FOLFOX plus bevacizumab, this was not feasible due to the unavailability of bevacizumab in the Brazilian public health system. Therefore, mFOLFIRINOX was selected to offer a higher expected response rate compared to FOLFOX alone.
After seven chemotherapy cycles (November 14, 2023–March 11, 2024), partial response was observed (Figure 1B and D) per RECIST v1.1,10 with marked respiratory symptom improvement.
Molecular tumor board
NGS was performed using a customized panel of 40 genes with SureSelect (Agilent) for library preparation chemistry on the Illumina MiSeq platform, with data analyzed using SureCall v.4.2 (Agilent) and the GRCh37 reference genome.
NGS results, available in March 2024 (after seven cycles of chemotherapy), identified an EGFR c.2573T>G p.(L858R) mutation in exon 21 with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of 5.2%. Given the imaging findings and the driver EGFR mutation, NSCLC was favored. Chemotherapy was paused, and an oral EGFR-TKI (gefitinib) was initiated two weeks after the seventh cycle.
Following gefitinib initiation, the patient experienced progressive respiratory worsening, with dyspnea and cough. One month later, he was admitted to the emergency department with significant dyspnea. New CT scans (Figure 2A and B) showed progressive lung disease with bronchial obstruction and new central nervous system lesions (Figure 3A and B). Cranial CT, rather than MRI, was performed due to greater accessibility and faster availability within the Brazilian public healthcare system.
At this stage, an expanded NGS panel was requested, revealing pathogenic variants in APC (c.1495C>T p.(R499*)) and TP53 (c.438G>A p.(W146*)), with VAF of 44.2% and 46.8%, respectively. These findings clarified the diagnosis as metastatic CRC with EGFR/APC co-mutation.
Patient update
On June 17, 2024, the patient underwent conformal (3D) radiotherapy to the left pulmonary hilum (800 cGy, single fraction) to relieve dyspnea. Despite symptom relief, his condition continued to decline, leading to palliative care initiation. He remained hospitalized for symptom control and died on August 04, 2024, 10 months after the metastatic adenocarcinoma diagnosis.
